posts.title: I made LLM context a user-editable DAG instead of an automatic memory layer
content: Most LLM memory systems automatically decide what to retrieve and inject.
I am experimenting with the opposite approach: make the context graph visible, and let the user edit it directly.

In ThoughtDAG, every question-and-answer exchange is a node. An incoming edge means that node is included in the next model request. Delete the edge, regenerate the same prompt, and that branch disappears from the actual context—not just from the visualization.

One piece of feedback I received was to add a small router model that suggests which edges are relevant. I can see the usability benefit, but I do not want context selection to become another hidden autonomous layer.
Would that preserve the value of explicit context control, or would you prefer fully automatic memory/RAG?

MIT-licensed repo:
https://github.com/chenxiachan/thoughtdag

Live example, no signup or key required:
https://app.thoughtdag.workers.dev/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=organic_social&utm_campaign=visible_context_2026_07&utm_content=llmdevs_manual_vs_auto
posts.hypothesis: LLM application developers will engage more with the manual-versus-automatic design tension than with a generic launch announcement.

content:
I deleted one wire and the LLM changed its answer—without changing the prompt.

In ThoughtDAG, the wires are the prompt.

Every node is one question/answer exchange.

When you ask from a node, ThoughtDAG walks only its upstream edges and turns those ancestors into the model input.

Delete an edge, and that branch is no longer remembered.

This is deliberately not an autonomous agent that silently manages memory.

The graph stays visible. The user decides what is included, merged, or pruned.

Open source, MIT licensed:
https://github.com/chenxiachan/thoughtdag

Try the example canvas:
https://app.thoughtdag.workers.dev/?utm_source=x&utm_medium=organic_social&utm_campaign=visible_context_2026_07&utm_content=delete_one_wire
posts.hypothesis: A causal visual demonstration will outperform a feature-list launch post on an owned technical account.

content:
Most LLM tools hide memory selection behind retrieval or an agent.

I built the opposite: a graph where context stays visible and editable.
Each edge carries real prompt context. Delete one wire, regenerate the same question, and the removed branch disappears from what the model sees.

ThoughtDAG is open source and human-controlled—not a workflow runner.

Repo: https://github.com/chenxiachan/thoughtdag
Demo: https://app.thoughtdag.workers.dev/?utm_source=bluesky&utm_medium=organic_social&utm_campaign=visible_context_2026_07&utm_content=context_not_hidden
posts.hypothesis: The open-web and research-tool audience will respond to inspectable context and human control.

content: What if an LLM's memory were something you could inspect and edit—not something an agent silently managed?
That is the interaction model I am testing with ThoughtDAG.
Every question-and-answer exchange becomes a node. The incoming edges are not decorative: they determine which upstream exchanges are included in the model's next request.
Delete one edge and regenerate the same prompt, and the deleted branch disappears from the actual context.
The interesting design tension is not graph versus chat. It is manual control versus automatic memory selection.

A model could suggest which context is relevant. But if it injects that context invisibly, the trust problem returns. My current direction is therefore model-suggested, human-approved context: assistance without surrendering inspectability.

ThoughtDAG is MIT licensed and available as an early open prototype.

Repository: https://github.com/chenxiachan/thoughtdag
Live example: https://app.thoughtdag.workers.dev/?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=organic_social&utm_campaign=visible_context_2026_07&utm_content=trust_mechanism
For people building long-running LLM interfaces: would you rather edit context manually, approve model suggestions, or delegate memory selection completely?
posts.hypothesis: The stronger personal account should amplify a design insight and external feedback, not repeat the launch announcement.
